# About Voz Cruda: Apparel Sourcing and Low MOQ Clothing in India

URL: https://vozcruda.com/about.html
Updated: 2026-10-24

**Short answer:** **Voz Cruda LLP** is an apparel sourcing company in Bengaluru, India. It matches fashion brands, boutiques, D2C sellers and private label businesses with suitable clothing manufacturers and coordinates production. Its service **Smallotz** lets small buyers order low MOQ clothing by pooling orders with other buyers until the factory's minimum order quantity is reached.

## What we do

Finding a factory is rarely the hard part of building a fashion brand. Finding one that fits your product, quantity and production needs is. Voz Cruda works on that problem in four steps:

- **Share your requirement:** product, quantity, budget, specifications and timeline.
- **Match with suppliers:** we find manufacturing options that fit your category, capability and volume.
- **Choose your path:** compare the most relevant options before you commit.
- **Produce and repeat:** we coordinate next steps and help build a process you can reorder from.

Our services are supplier matching, MOQ aggregation (order pooling), production coordination and private label sourcing.

## Smallotz: low MOQ clothing by order pooling

Factories set minimum order quantities that small brands often cannot reach on their own. [Smallotz](https://smallotz.vozcruda.com/) pools your order with other buyers making the same kind of product, so together you reach the factory MOQ and each of you orders only what you need. That gives small brands access to factory production runs, keeps less cash locked in stock, and makes it practical to test new styles in small lots and reorder what sells. Read more in [What is MOQ aggregation?](https://vozcruda.com/what-is-moq-aggregation.html)

## What we source

- **T-shirts and tops:** knits, basics, graphic tees
- **Shirts:** casual, formal, resort
- **Bottomwear:** denim, trousers, joggers
- **Dresses:** day, occasion, co-ords
- **Ethnic wear:** kurtas, sets, fusion
- **Outerwear:** jackets, hoodies, layers
- **Private label** and **custom** requirements

## Who we work with

We work with apparel businesses that do not have their own sourcing department: emerging fashion brands making their first collection, growing apparel businesses adding manufacturing options, and private label businesses sourcing products under their own brand. On the supply side, we are building a network of manufacturers matched by real product capability.

## Where we source in India

We build around the regions where India makes clothes: **Tiruppur** (knitwear and basics), **Surat** (synthetic and woven apparel), **Jaipur** (ethnic wear and fashion), **Delhi NCR** (fashion and private label) and **Bengaluru** (contemporary apparel). See our guide to [India's apparel manufacturing hubs](https://vozcruda.com/india-apparel-manufacturing-hubs.html).

## Our own label

Alongside sourcing, Voz Cruda makes its own contemporary streetwear, released as curated drops at the [Voz Cruda Store](https://shop.vozcruda.com/).

## Company details

- **Legal name:** Voz Cruda LLP
- **Registered office:** Balaji Arcade, 2nd & 3rd Floor, A.V.S. Compound, 20th L Cross Road, AVS Layout, 4th Block, Ejipura, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India

# Clothing Cost and Price Calculator: Cost per Piece, MRP and Profit

URL: https://vozcruda.com/clothing-cost-calculator.html
Updated: 2026-10-24

**Short answer:** Your **landed cost** is everything it takes to get one finished, packed piece into your hands. Your **selling price** is landed cost times your markup, and your **MRP** adds GST on top. What you keep is the selling price minus landed cost and the cost of selling each order (shipping, fees, returns and marketing). Fill in the calculator below to get your own numbers.

## How the calculator works

It follows the same method as our guide on [how to price your clothing products](https://vozcruda.com/how-to-price-clothing-products.html):

- **Landed cost per piece** = fabric and making + printing + labels and trims + packaging + (freight + sampling) ÷ order quantity.
- **Selling price before GST** = landed cost × your markup.
- **Suggested MRP** = selling price + GST, rounded up to a price ending in 49 or 99.
- **Cost to sell one order** = shipping + fees (as a % of MRP) + return rate × cost per return + marketing per order.
- **Profit per order** = selling price before GST − landed cost − cost to sell one order.

If you already have a price in mind, type it into **Or test your own MRP** and the calculator shows the profit at that price instead.

## What to put in each field

- **Fabric and making:** the factory's per-piece price for the garment. If you buy fabric yourself, add fabric cost per piece and the CMT (cut, make, trim) charge.
- **Printing or embroidery:** per piece, at your quantity. Small runs cost more per piece; see [screen printing vs DTF vs DTG](https://vozcruda.com/screen-printing-vs-dtf-vs-dtg-india.html).
- **One-off costs:** anything you pay once per order, like freight, sampling and tech pack work. The calculator spreads them over your quantity.
- **Cost per return:** reverse shipping plus the forward shipping you lose and the cost of repacking.
- **Marketing per order:** your monthly ad and creator spend divided by monthly orders.

## Ways to improve the numbers

- **Lower landed cost without cutting quality:** stick to standard fabrics and trims, and avoid below-MOQ surcharges by pooling your order on Smallotz.
- **Cut returns:** an accurate size chart and honest photos reduce size-related returns.
- **Push prepaid orders:** cash-on-delivery adds charges and cancellations.
- **Price per channel:** marketplaces take commission and see more returns, so they usually need a higher multiple than your own site.

Smallotz by Voz Cruda

### Get a real production cost for your cost sheet.

Order factory-made clothing in the quantity you need. Smallotz pools your order with other buyers so the lot reaches the factory MOQ, and the per-piece price stays close to bulk.

[Open Smallotz ↗](https://smallotz.vozcruda.com/)

## Frequently asked questions

**How do I calculate the cost of a clothing product?**
Add everything it takes to get one finished, packed piece into your hands: fabric and making, printing or embroidery, labels and trims, packaging, and your freight and sampling costs divided by the number of pieces. That total is your landed cost per piece.

**What markup should a clothing brand use?**
Many D2C brands price at around three to four times landed cost, because shipping, returns, payment fees and marketing come out of the selling price. Selling on marketplaces usually needs a higher multiple. Use the calculator to check that your markup still leaves profit after selling costs.

**Is MRP inclusive of GST in India?**
Yes. MRP is the maximum retail price including all taxes. This calculator adds the GST rate you enter on top of your selling price to suggest an MRP. GST rates on clothing depend on the product and its price, so confirm the current rate for your HSN code with your accountant.

**Why is my profit so low even with a 3x markup?**
Usually because of marketing cost per order, returns or marketplace fees. Try lowering returns with a better size chart, pushing prepaid orders, or raising the markup for marketplaces. A lower landed cost from pooled production also helps.

**How can a small brand lower its cost per piece?**
Spread fixed costs like sampling and freight over more pieces, keep to standard fabrics and trims, and avoid below-MOQ surcharges by pooling your order with other buyers on Smallotz, which keeps the per-piece price close to bulk.

# Free Tech Pack Template for Clothing Brands (Excel, Google Sheets and PDF)

URL: https://vozcruda.com/tech-pack-template.html
Updated: 2026-10-24

**Short answer:** Download the free tech pack template below as an **Excel file** (also opens in Google Sheets and Numbers) or a **printable PDF**. It has the eight parts factories expect: cover, flat sketches, size chart with tolerances, bill of materials, construction, artwork and placement, labels and packing, and an order sheet. A filled-in t-shirt example is included so you can see what good looks like.

## What is in the template

| Sheet | What you fill in | Why the factory needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Cover | Brand, style name and number, drop, version, sizes, quantity, contact | Everyone refers to the same garment and version |
| 2. Flat sketches | Front and back drawings with numbered callouts | Shows what is intentional, like a dropped shoulder |
| 3. Size chart | Points of measure for each size, with tolerances | Finished garments are checked against it |
| 4. Bill of materials | Fabric, GSM, composition, rib, thread, labels, trims | Accurate quotes and the right materials in bulk |
| 5. Construction | Seam types, stitch types, hem widths, finishes | Stops quiet changes between sample and bulk |
| 6. Artwork | Print or embroidery method, file, size, placement, colours | Repeatable placement across sizes and reorders |
| 7. Labels and packing | Neck and care labels, hang tags, fold, polybag, cartons | Avoids last-minute dispatch delays |
| 8. Order sheet | Quantity per colour and size, delivery date and address | Lets the factory plan fabric and production |

## How to fill it in

- **Start with the cover.** Give the style a number (for example TS-001) and call the first issue V1.
- **Measure a garment you like** for the size chart, laid flat, in centimetres. Grade the other sizes from it and add a tolerance for each point.
- **Be specific in the bill of materials.** Write "100% combed cotton single jersey, 240 GSM, bio-washed", not "cotton". Our [fabric and GSM guide](https://vozcruda.com/fabric-guide-for-clothing-brands.html) explains the terms.
- **Measure placements.** "Top of print 8 cm below front neck seam" instead of "print on chest".
- **Attach artwork as separate files**, not only as pictures inside the tech pack.
- **Send it with your quantity and target date** so the factory can quote properly, then review each sample against it and issue V2 with changes. See the [sampling process](https://vozcruda.com/clothing-sampling-process-india.html).

New to tech packs? Read [what a tech pack is and how to make one](https://vozcruda.com/tech-pack-guide-for-beginners.html), then follow the [page-by-page t-shirt example](https://vozcruda.com/tech-pack-example-t-shirt.html). Once you have a cost per piece, check your pricing with the [clothing cost and price calculator](https://vozcruda.com/clothing-cost-calculator.html).

Smallotz by Voz Cruda

### Tech pack ready? Order only what you need.

Smallotz pools your order with other buyers making the same kind of product, so together you reach the factory MOQ and each brand orders only its own quantity.

[Open Smallotz ↗](https://smallotz.vozcruda.com/)

## Frequently asked questions

**What should a tech pack include?**
A cover page with style number and version, front and back flat sketches with callouts, a size chart with tolerances, a bill of materials, construction details, artwork and placement, labels and packing instructions, and an order sheet with quantities by colour and size.

**Can I use this tech pack template in Google Sheets?**
Yes. Download the Excel file, then in Google Drive choose New, File upload, and open it with Google Sheets. All sheets and formulas carry over.

**Do I need a designer to make a tech pack?**
Not for simple products like t-shirts and hoodies. Measure a garment you like for the size chart, draw simple flat sketches or trace a photo, and fill in each sheet. A designer helps for complex styles.

**Is this template only for t-shirts?**
No. The structure works for most garments. The example file is a t-shirt; for a hoodie add hood, cuff, waistband rib and pocket measurements, and for a shirt add collar, cuff and button details.

**Can I send this tech pack to Voz Cruda for a quote?**
Yes. Send your completed tech pack with your quantity and target date through the sourcing request form or to sales@vozcruda.com, and Voz Cruda will match it with a suitable manufacturer, or a pooled lot on Smallotz for small quantities.

# Low MOQ Clothing Manufacturers in India: How to Order Small Batches in 2026

URL: https://vozcruda.com/low-moq-clothing-manufacturers-india.html
Updated: 2026-10-24

**Short answer:** Low MOQ clothing means ordering garments from a manufacturer in small quantities, typically under 100 to 150 pieces per style. In India you can get there three ways: small job-work units (higher prices), factories that charge a below-MOQ surcharge, or **order pooling**, where several brands combine orders to meet one factory's minimum. Voz Cruda runs pooled lots through [Smallotz](https://smallotz.vozcruda.com/).

If you have emailed a garment factory as a new brand, you have probably heard some version of "our minimum is 500 pieces per style, per colour." For a first drop, a boutique restock or a test of a new silhouette, that number can lock lakhs of rupees into stock you are not yet sure will sell.

This guide covers what MOQs look like across categories in India, why factories set them, and every realistic way to order below them, including the one we built Smallotz around.

## What is low MOQ? MOQ meaning in clothing

**MOQ (minimum order quantity)** is the smallest order a manufacturer will accept for one product. In apparel it is usually set per style, and often per colour too. A factory quoting "300 pieces MOQ, 100 per colour" means you need at least three colours of 100 pieces each.

**Low MOQ** simply means that minimum is small. In Indian garment manufacturing, people usually say low MOQ for anything under about 100 to 150 pieces per style. Some suppliers advertise low MOQ but apply it per style and per colour, or only on their stock fabrics, so always ask what the number covers.

### The MOQs you will hear

| Type of minimum | What it means |
|---|---|
| Per style | Total pieces of one design, across all colours and sizes |
| Per colour | Minimum pieces in each colour of that style |
| Fabric MOQ | The mill or trader's minimum for a custom fabric or dye colour, often in kilos or metres |
| Print or embroidery MOQ | The minimum the print or embroidery unit accepts per design |
| Trims MOQ | Minimums for custom labels, tags, zips or buttons |

The real minimum for your order is usually the highest of these. A factory may happily sew 100 pieces, but if your custom colour needs a full dye lot, the fabric minimum decides.

### Why factories set minimums

Factories are not being difficult. Every production run has costs that stay the same whether they make 50 pieces or 5,000:

- **Line setup:** grading patterns, setting markers, adjusting machines and briefing tailors.
- **Fabric minimums:** mills and traders sell by the roll or by a minimum dye lot, so small orders leave expensive leftovers.
- **Dyeing and printing:** a dye batch, a set of screens or an embroidery program costs the same regardless of quantity.
- **Trims:** custom labels, tags and packaging are sold in bulk lots.
- **Overheads:** sampling, paperwork and quality checks for every order.

Below the MOQ, those fixed costs are spread over too few pieces. The factory either loses money or quotes a price you cannot sell at.

## Typical MOQs by clothing category in India

MOQs vary by factory, fabric and finish, so treat these as the ranges you are likely to hear, not fixed rules.

| Category | Common factory MOQ per style | What drives it |
|---|---|---|
| T-shirts and basic knits | 300 to 1,000 pieces | Knitted fabric and dye lots, screen setup |
| Hoodies and sweatshirts | 200 to 500 pieces | Fleece fabric minimums, rib matching |
| Shirts (woven) | 200 to 500 pieces | Fabric minimums, buttons and collar interlining |
| Denim and trousers | 300 to 1,000 pieces | Washing runs, hardware like rivets and zips |
| Kurtas and ethnic wear | 100 to 300 pieces | Printing or dyeing batches, handwork |
| Dresses and co-ords | 100 to 300 pieces | Fabric, pattern complexity |

Category guides: [t-shirts](https://vozcruda.com/small-batch-t-shirt-manufacturing-india.html), [hoodies](https://vozcruda.com/low-moq-hoodie-manufacturer-india.html), [kidswear](https://vozcruda.com/low-moq-kidswear-manufacturers-india.html) and [ethnic wear](https://vozcruda.com/low-moq-ethnic-wear-manufacturers-india.html).

Many factories also set a **per-colour minimum**. If you want a tee in four colours, check whether the MOQ applies to the style or to each colour.

## Five ways to get low MOQ clothing, compared

Every route to small-batch clothing trades something away. The question is which trade-off suits your brand right now.

| Route | Typical quantity | Price per piece | Customisation | Main trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Print-on-demand | 1 piece | Highest | Prints on stock blanks | Thin margins, no custom fit or fabric |
| Wholesale blanks + local print | 10 to 50 | High | Print, neck labels | Same blanks as many other brands |
| Small job-work or sampling units | 30 to 100 | High | Full | Limited capacity, inconsistent quality |
| Factory with below-MOQ surcharge | Below MOQ | Very high | Full | Surcharge can wipe out your margin |
| Order pooling (Smallotz) | What you need | Close to bulk | Shared base product, your quantity, your branding | Wait while the lot fills |

### When each route makes sense

- **Print-on-demand** works for testing designs with zero stock risk, but rarely builds a premium brand.
- **Job-work units** suit fully custom pieces in very small numbers, if you can supervise quality closely.
- **Pooling** suits brands that want factory quality and near-bulk pricing on proven product types, like heavyweight tees, hoodies, joggers or basic shirts.

## How order pooling works

Order pooling, also called MOQ aggregation, lets several buyers share one production run. The factory sees one order that meets its minimum. Each buyer pays for, and receives, only their share.

Here is a simple example. A Tiruppur knitwear unit has an MOQ of 500 pieces for a 240 GSM oversized cotton tee. Your brand needs 120. Alone, you are 380 pieces short and most factories will say no. In a pooled lot, three other buyers add 80, 120 and 180 pieces. The lot reaches 500, production goes ahead, and every brand pays a per-piece price close to the bulk rate.

### What stays shared and what stays yours

In a pooled lot the **base product** is shared: the garment type, fabric, GSM and construction. Your quantity, size split and, depending on the lot, colours, prints and labels can be your own. That is what keeps setup costs shared while your product still looks like your brand.

## How to order low MOQ clothing step by step

- **Define the product clearly.** Garment type, fabric and GSM, fit, sizes, colours and any print or embroidery. A simple tech pack helps. See our [beginner's tech pack guide](https://vozcruda.com/tech-pack-guide-for-beginners.html).
- **Pick your quantity per style.** Start with what you can sell in 6 to 10 weeks. Reorder winners instead of guessing big.
- **Choose your route.** Under about 300 pieces per style, a pooled lot on Smallotz is usually the most cost-effective. Above that, Voz Cruda can match you with a factory directly.
- **Approve a sample.** Check fabric hand-feel, measurements, stitching and print quality before bulk production.
- **Confirm in writing.** Quantity, size split, price, delivery date and quality standard on a purchase order, not only a WhatsApp chat.
- **Inspect on arrival and reorder.** Count, measure and check a sample of pieces. Then reorder the styles that sold.

## How to get a lower MOQ from a factory

Minimums are often negotiable when you remove what causes them. Choosing the factory's stock fabric instead of a custom dye, ordering fewer colours, using the same fabric across two styles and keeping trims standard can all bring the number down. Offering a clear reorder plan or a flexible delivery date helps too. Our guide on [how to negotiate MOQ with clothing manufacturers](https://vozcruda.com/how-to-negotiate-moq-clothing-manufacturers.html) covers each tactic and includes a message you can send.

## Questions to ask any low MOQ supplier

- Is the MOQ per style, per colour, or per fabric?
- What is the price at my quantity, and what would it be at 2x and 5x?
- How much does a sample cost, and is it adjusted against the bulk order?
- What is the lead time after sample approval?
- What happens if pieces fail measurements or have defects?
- Can I reorder the same product later at the same quantity?

For a deeper checklist, read [how to vet apparel suppliers](https://vozcruda.com/how-to-vet-apparel-suppliers.html).

## The bottom line

Factory MOQs exist for good reasons, but they no longer have to decide whether your brand can launch. If you need a few hundred pieces of something unique, a small unit may suit you. If you want factory quality at close to bulk pricing in the quantity you can actually sell, pool your order. [Start on Smallotz](https://smallotz.vozcruda.com/) or [tell Voz Cruda what you want to make](https://vozcruda.com/#contact).

## Frequently asked questions

**What is low MOQ?**
Low MOQ means a low minimum order quantity: the supplier accepts small orders. In clothing manufacturing it usually means under 100 to 150 pieces per style, where many factories ask for 300 to 1,000 or more.

**What does low MOQ mean in clothing?**
MOQ is the minimum order quantity a factory accepts per style. Low MOQ usually means under 100 to 150 pieces per style, compared with the 300 to 1,000+ pieces many garment factories ask for.

**Which clothing manufacturers in India accept small orders?**
Small job-work units, sampling studios and some knitwear units in Tiruppur and Delhi NCR accept small orders, usually at a higher price per piece. Order pooling platforms such as Smallotz let you reach a regular factory's MOQ by combining your order with other buyers.

**Can I order 50 pieces from a garment factory?**
Most mid-size factories will decline or charge a surcharge for 50 pieces of one style. You can get 50 pieces at near-bulk pricing by joining a pooled lot, where other buyers make up the rest of the factory's minimum.

**What is the difference between low MOQ and no MOQ?**
Low MOQ means the factory still has a minimum, just a small one. No MOQ means you can order any quantity, even one piece, which is how print-on-demand works. Pooled lots on Smallotz feel like no MOQ to the buyer because other buyers fill the factory minimum.

**What is a good MOQ for a new clothing brand?**
Order what you expect to sell in 6 to 10 weeks. For many first drops that is somewhere between 30 and 150 pieces per style, then reorder the styles that sell instead of guessing big upfront.

**Is low MOQ clothing more expensive?**
Ordering alone below MOQ usually costs more per piece because setup, cutting and fabric minimums are spread over fewer units. Pooling spreads those fixed costs across the whole lot, so the per-piece price stays close to bulk.

**How long does a low MOQ order take?**
Plan for 4 to 10 weeks from approved sample to delivery for most basics, depending on fabric availability and print or embroidery work. A pooled lot also needs time to fill, which is usually faster for popular products like t-shirts and hoodies.

# What Is MOQ Aggregation? How Order Pooling Helps Small Clothing Brands

URL: https://vozcruda.com/what-is-moq-aggregation.html
Updated: 2026-10-10

**Short answer:** **MOQ aggregation**, also called order pooling, means combining orders from several buyers so that together they meet a factory's minimum order quantity. The factory runs one efficient production order; each buyer receives only the pieces they committed to, at a price close to bulk.

Minimum order quantities are one of the biggest barriers for small fashion brands in India. A brand that can sell 100 hoodies a season cannot place a 500-piece order without tying up cash in stock it does not need. MOQ aggregation solves the mismatch from the other side: instead of asking the factory to lower its minimum, it brings the factory more buyers.

## How MOQ aggregation works

In apparel, a pooled order usually runs in five stages:

- **A base product is defined.** For example, a 240 GSM oversized cotton t-shirt made by a knitwear unit in Tiruppur, with a 500-piece minimum.
- **Buyers commit quantities.** Each brand adds the number of pieces it wants, along with its size split and any options the lot allows.
- **The lot fills.** Commitments add up until the combined quantity reaches the factory MOQ.
- **Production runs as one order.** Fabric is bought, cut and stitched as a single run, which is what keeps unit costs low.
- **Each buyer receives their share.** Pieces are sorted, packed and dispatched per brand.

### A worked example

| Buyer | Pieces committed | Running total |
|---|---|---|
| Your brand | 120 | 120 of 500 |
| Instagram label, Pune | 80 | 200 of 500 |
| Boutique, Kochi | 120 | 320 of 500 |
| D2C brand, Delhi | 180 | 500 of 500 |
| Result | Lot full. Production goes ahead. |

The buyers here are illustrative. The point is that none of them could reach 500 pieces alone, and all of them get factory pricing together.

## What is shared and what stays yours

Aggregation only works if the parts of a garment that drive setup cost are shared. Everything else can be individual.

| Usually shared across the lot | Often yours to choose |
|---|---|
| Garment type and pattern block | Quantity and size split |
| Fabric composition and GSM | Colour, where the lot offers several |
| Construction and stitching spec | Neck labels, hang tags and packaging |
| Factory and production timeline | Prints or embroidery, where supported |

Because customers see your print, your label and your branding, two brands in the same lot can still look completely different on the shelf.

## Why factories like pooled orders

Factories set MOQs because a production run has fixed costs: line setup, fabric minimums, dye batches and screens. A pooled lot meets that minimum, so the run is just as efficient as one from a large buyer. For the factory, aggregation means:

- Filled capacity during slower months.
- Orders that meet their MOQ without negotiating with dozens of small buyers.
- Access to a pipeline of growing brands that may become direct customers later.

## MOQ aggregation vs ordering alone

|  | Ordering alone below MOQ | Pooled lot |
|---|---|---|
| Will the factory accept it? | Often not | Yes, once the lot is full |
| Price per piece | Higher, or a surcharge | Close to bulk |
| Cash tied up in stock | Low if accepted, but rarely possible | Only what you commit |
| Design freedom | Full | Within the shared base product |
| Timeline | Production only | Lot fill time + production |

## Risks and how to manage them

- **Fill time.** A lot for a niche product may take longer to fill. Popular basics fill faster. Plan launches with this buffer.
- **Less design freedom.** You work within the shared base. If you need a unique fabric or pattern, a direct factory order may suit you better.
- **Quality consistency.** Because one factory makes the whole lot, quality depends on that factory. Look for a coordinator who checks quality before dispatch.
- **Clear terms.** Understand how long the lot stays open, when you pay, and what happens if specifications change.

## When MOQ aggregation is the right choice

Pooling is a strong fit when you need fewer than about 300 pieces per style, you are selling proven product types like tees, hoodies, joggers or shirts, and you care about factory quality and margin. It is less suited to one-off couture pieces or garments built on a fabric no one else is using.

Ready to try it? Read the full [guide to low MOQ clothing in India](https://vozcruda.com/low-moq-clothing-manufacturers-india.html), or [open Smallotz](https://smallotz.vozcruda.com/) and add your quantity to a lot.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is MOQ aggregation?**
MOQ aggregation is combining orders from several buyers so that together they meet a manufacturer's minimum order quantity. Each buyer pays for and receives only their own share of the production run.

**Is MOQ aggregation the same as group buying?**
They are closely related. Group buying usually means buyers getting a discount on a finished product. MOQ aggregation is about getting into a production run at all, by pooling quantities of a product that is made after the lot fills.

**Can I still have my own brand label in a pooled order?**
Usually yes. The base garment, fabric and construction are shared, while labels, prints and colours can often be specified per buyer, depending on the lot. Check what is customisable before you join.

**What happens if a pooled lot does not fill?**
That depends on the platform's terms. On Smallotz, production goes ahead once the lot reaches the factory's minimum. Before you commit, check how long a lot stays open and what happens to your order if it does not fill.

**Who benefits from MOQ aggregation?**
Buyers get factory pricing without buying hundreds of units. Factories fill production capacity with orders that meet their MOQ, from customers they could not serve one by one.

# How to Start a Clothing Brand in India with Low Investment

URL: https://vozcruda.com/start-clothing-brand-low-investment-india.html
Updated: 2026-10-10

**Short answer:** To start a clothing brand in India on a small budget: pick a narrow niche, launch 2 to 4 styles, produce them in small quantities through a low MOQ route such as order pooling, sell through Instagram and your own store first, and reinvest in reorders of the styles that sell. Stock is your biggest cost, so keeping your first drop small keeps your investment small.

The most common way new fashion brands run out of money is not bad design. It is buying too much stock too early. A factory asks for 500 pieces per style, the founder orders three styles, and suddenly most of the budget is sitting in cartons. This plan is built to avoid that.

## Step 1: Choose a niche you can describe in one line

"Clothing for everyone" is impossible to market on a small budget. A narrow niche makes every rupee of marketing work harder. Good niches combine a customer, a product and a reason to buy:

- Heavyweight oversized basics for college students in tier-2 cities.
- Breathable co-ord sets for working women in humid cities.
- Minimal graphic tees for indie music fans.

Check that people already buy in that space: look at Instagram pages, marketplace reviews and what competitors restock.

## Step 2: Keep your first drop small

Launch **2 to 4 styles** in 2 or 3 colours each. A small drop is cheaper to produce, easier to shoot and gives you clean data. If one style sells out and another sits, you have learned something worth more than a big collection.

Rule of thumbOrder what you can realistically sell in 6 to 10 weeks. Reordering a winner is cheaper than discounting dead stock.

## Step 3: Get the product right before you buy stock

- **Write a simple tech pack:** sketches, measurements per size, fabric, GSM, colours and print placement. Our [tech pack guide](https://vozcruda.com/tech-pack-guide-for-beginners.html) walks through it.
- **Order samples:** expect one or two rounds. Wear-test and wash-test them.
- **Fix the size chart:** fit problems are the top reason for returns in online fashion.

## Step 4: Produce in low MOQ

This is where most of your budget goes, so the route matters. Your main options:

| Route | Good for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Print-on-demand | Testing designs with no stock | Low margin, generic blanks |
| Small job-work unit | Fully custom pieces in very small runs | Higher unit cost, quality varies |
| Pooled lot on Smallotz | Factory quality on basics at near-bulk price | Lot needs time to fill |
| Direct factory order | 300+ pieces per style | Large cash commitment |

For a deeper comparison, read [low MOQ clothing manufacturers in India](https://vozcruda.com/low-moq-clothing-manufacturers-india.html).

## Step 5: Budget for more than production

Founders often budget for stock and forget everything around it. Plan a line for each of these:

- **Samples and tech pack:** sampling rounds, courier and any design help.
- **Production:** pieces, labels, tags, polybags and boxes.
- **Brand basics:** logo, trademark application through IP India, website and domain.
- **Photography:** product and on-model shots. This sells more than any ad.
- **Marketing:** creator collaborations and a small paid ads test.
- **Operations:** shipping partner, payment gateway fees and returns.
- **Buffer:** keep money aside for the reorder of your best seller.

To turn these lines into a selling price, see [how to price your clothing products](https://vozcruda.com/how-to-price-clothing-products.html).

## Step 6: Set up the business basics

- Choose a structure: sole proprietorship, partnership, LLP or private limited company.
- Open a business bank account.
- Check GST registration requirements with a chartered accountant, especially before selling on marketplaces.
- Register on the Udyam portal to be recognised as an MSME.
- Search and file your brand name as a trademark early.

## Step 7: Sell where your customers already are

- **Instagram first:** build interest before launch with behind-the-scenes posts from sampling and production.
- **Your own store:** a Shopify or similar store keeps your margin and customer data.
- **Marketplaces later:** Myntra, Ajio and others add reach but come with commissions and return costs.
- **Pop-ups and flea markets:** great for feedback and cash flow in your own city.

## Step 8: Reorder fast, expand slowly

Track sell-through by style, colour and size. When something sells, reorder it quickly, in a pooled lot or directly once volumes grow. Add new styles one or two at a time. Brands that grow on reorders keep their cash moving and avoid the dead-stock trap.

Want help with the manufacturing side? [Tell Voz Cruda what you want to make](https://vozcruda.com/#contact) and we will suggest the right route for your quantity.

## Frequently asked questions

**How much money do I need to start a clothing brand in India?**
It depends mostly on how much stock you buy. Production is the largest cost, so the smaller your first drop, the smaller your investment. Low MOQ ordering and pooled lots let you start with tens of pieces per style instead of hundreds.

**Can I start a clothing brand without a factory MOQ of 500 pieces?**
Yes. You can use print-on-demand, small job-work units, or order pooling. Pooling on Smallotz lets you order factory-made pieces in small quantities by combining your order with other buyers.

**How many designs should my first collection have?**
Most first-time founders do better with 2 to 4 styles in a few colours than with a large collection. A tight drop is cheaper to produce, easier to photograph and market, and gives clearer data on what sells.

**Do I need GST registration to sell clothing online in India?**
Registration rules depend on your turnover, where you sell and which marketplaces you use, and they change from time to time. Speak to a chartered accountant before your first sale, especially if you plan to sell on marketplaces.

**What clothing products are best for a first brand?**
Products with steady demand and simple construction, such as t-shirts, hoodies, sweatshirts and joggers, are easiest to launch. They are widely produced, which also makes them well suited to pooled low MOQ lots.

# How to Launch a Private Label Clothing Brand in India

URL: https://vozcruda.com/private-label-clothing-brand-india.html
Updated: 2026-10-10

**Short answer:** A **private label clothing brand** sells garments made by a manufacturer under your own brand name. You start from a proven product, customise the details that matter (fabric, colour, fit, print, labels, packaging) and sell it as yours. It is faster and cheaper than designing every piece from scratch, and in India it can now start at low MOQ.

## Private label vs white label vs custom design

These three terms get mixed up. The difference is how much of the product you change.

| Model | What you change | Speed to launch | Brand uniqueness |
|---|---|---|---|
| White label | Only your label and packaging | Fastest | Low |
| Private label | Labels plus fabric, colour, print, fit tweaks | Fast | Medium to high |
| Full custom design | Everything, from pattern to fabric | Slowest | Highest |

Most successful small brands start with private label on a few hero products, then move into custom design once they know what their customers want.

## Step 1: Pick your hero products

Choose two or three products your niche buys again and again. For most streetwear and casual brands that means heavyweight tees, hoodies, sweatshirts or joggers. For womenswear it could be co-ord sets, kurtas or shirts. Fewer products means lower MOQ pressure and a clearer brand.

## Step 2: Decide what to customise

- **Fabric and GSM:** for example, 240 GSM cotton for a premium oversized tee.
- **Fit:** oversized, boxy, regular or cropped. Small changes to body length and sleeve make a big difference.
- **Colour:** your signature shades.
- **Decoration:** screen print, DTF print, puff print or embroidery.
- **Branding:** woven neck labels or printed neck labels, wash care labels, hang tags and packaging.

## Step 3: Find the right private label manufacturer

Match the product to the region that specialises in it. Tiruppur leads in knitwear like tees and hoodies; Surat in synthetics and wovens; Jaipur in ethnic wear and prints; Delhi NCR in fashion and private label. Read our guide to [India's apparel hubs](https://vozcruda.com/india-apparel-manufacturing-hubs.html) for more.

When you speak to manufacturers, confirm:

- They make your exact product category regularly.
- MOQ per style and per colour, plus minimums for labels and tags.
- Sampling cost and time.
- Whether they can source your fabric or need you to supply it.

Use our checklist on [how to vet apparel suppliers](https://vozcruda.com/how-to-vet-apparel-suppliers.html) before you commit.

## Step 4: Build your brand kit

Private label lives or dies on how branded it feels. Prepare:

- Logo files in vector format for labels and prints.
- Neck label design, with size and fibre content.
- Wash care label with fibre composition and care instructions.
- Hang tag and price tag design.
- Packaging: polybag, mailer box or tissue and sticker.

Check the labelling requirements that apply to your products and channels, such as fibre content, size, maker details and MRP for retail sales.

## Step 5: Sample, then produce

Approve a pre-production sample with your exact fabric, print and labels. Compare it against your tech pack measurements. Only then confirm bulk production on a written purchase order with quantity, size split, price and delivery date.

## Step 6: Launch and reorder

Shoot strong product photos, launch on Instagram and your own store, and track which sizes and colours sell. Reorder winners fast. Once a style regularly sells a few hundred units per run, you can move it from pooled lots to a direct factory order through Voz Cruda.

## Private label launch checklist

- Niche and 2 to 3 hero products chosen
- Customisation decided: fabric, GSM, fit, colours, decoration
- Manufacturer or pooled lot selected
- Brand kit ready: logo, labels, tags, packaging
- Sample approved against tech pack
- Purchase order confirmed in writing
- Photos, store and launch plan ready

Need help finding the right private label partner? [Send us your requirement](https://vozcruda.com/#contact).

## Frequently asked questions

**What is private label clothing?**
Private label clothing is made by a manufacturer but sold under your brand. You choose or adapt a proven product, then add your own labels, tags, packaging and often your own colours, prints or small design changes.

**What is the difference between private label and white label?**
White label means buying a ready-made product and simply adding your brand, with no changes to the product. Private label usually involves some customisation, such as fabric, colour, fit tweaks or prints, made exclusively for your brand.

**What is the MOQ for private label clothing in India?**
Many factories ask for 100 to 500 pieces per style for private label, plus minimums on custom woven labels and tags. Pooled lots on Smallotz let you start with smaller quantities by sharing the base product with other brands.

**Do I need my own designs for private label?**
No. You can start from a manufacturer's existing product and customise it. Many brands begin this way and move to fully custom designs once they understand their customers.

**Which private label products are easiest to start with?**
Basics with steady demand, such as t-shirts, hoodies, sweatshirts, joggers and shirts, are the easiest. Their production is well established and they are simple to brand with prints, embroidery and labels.

# How to Vet Apparel Suppliers in India: Quality, Reliability and Red Flags

URL: https://vozcruda.com/how-to-vet-apparel-suppliers.html
Updated: 2026-10-10

**Short answer:** To vet an apparel supplier in India: confirm they regularly make your exact product, verify their GST registration and factory address, speak to existing clients, order a paid sample and test it, agree everything in a written purchase order, and use staged payments rather than full advance. Walk away if any of these are refused.

Two factories in the same city making the same garment can deliver very different quality, timelines and communication. For a small brand, one bad order can mean returns, delays and a lost season. Vetting takes a few days. Skipping it can take months to recover from.

Still building a shortlist? Start with [how to find clothing manufacturers in India](https://vozcruda.com/how-to-find-clothing-manufacturers-india.html).

## 1. Check capability first

The most common mistake is choosing a supplier that can make clothes, but not your clothes. Ask:

- Which categories do you produce every month? Ask for photos of current production, not a catalogue.
- Do you knit, dye, print and stitch in-house, or outsource some steps? Outsourcing is common, but you should know who does what.
- What is your monthly capacity, and how much is free in my timeline?
- What is your MOQ per style and per colour?

## 2. Verify the business

| What to check | How |
|---|---|
| GST registration | Search their GSTIN on the official GST portal and match the legal name and address. |
| Factory address | Visit, or ask for a live video walk-through of the production floor. |
| Client references | Ask for two or three brands they currently supply and speak to them. |
| Online presence | Look for consistent details across their website, directory listings and reviews. |
| Who makes your goods | Confirm whether the person you deal with is the factory or a middleman. |

## 3. Order a paid sample and test it properly

A sample is the single best predictor of bulk quality. Pay for it, and test it like a customer would:

- **Measure** every point on your size chart. Tolerances of about 1 cm are common; agree yours in advance.
- **Feel and weigh** the fabric. Ask for the GSM and check it matches.
- **Inspect stitching:** even seams, no loose threads, secure hems and necklines.
- **Check decoration:** print sharpness, colour accuracy and embroidery density.
- **Wash it** three to five times. Look for shrinkage, colour bleeding, pilling and twisting.

Our [tech pack guide](https://vozcruda.com/tech-pack-guide-for-beginners.html) shows how to write specifications a factory can check against.

## 4. Ask the questions that reveal reliability

- What is the lead time after sample approval, and what usually causes delays?
- How do you handle defects or pieces that fail measurements?
- Will bulk use the same fabric lot as the sample?
- Who is my single point of contact, and how often will I get updates?
- Can I see the goods, or photos and videos, before dispatch?

Clear, specific answers are a good sign. Vague answers are not.

## 5. Put everything in writing

WhatsApp messages are useful but not enough. A purchase order should include:

- Style, fabric, GSM, colours and decoration, referencing the approved sample.
- Quantity and size split.
- Unit price, taxes and what is included (labels, packing, freight).
- Delivery date and the agreed quality standard.
- Payment terms and what happens with defects.

## 6. Use safer payment terms

With a new supplier, avoid paying 100% upfront. A deposit to start production and the balance after you approve finished goods is common and protects both sides. For larger orders, an inspection before the final payment is worth the cost.

## Red flags: when to walk away

- Refuses to make a sample, or wants a large order before showing quality.
- Quotes change after you agree, or extras appear late.
- No verifiable GST details or factory address.
- Pushes for full advance payment and urgency.
- Cannot name current clients or show current production.
- Avoids written purchase orders.
- Sample quality is far above what bulk pricing could realistically support.

## Or let a sourcing partner do the vetting

Vetting many suppliers is time-consuming for a founder who also has to design, market and sell. Voz Cruda matches brands with manufacturers based on product capability, quantity and requirements, then coordinates production through one point of contact. For small quantities, Smallotz pools your order into a lot that meets a vetted factory's minimum. [Start a sourcing request](https://vozcruda.com/#contact).

## Frequently asked questions

**How do I know if a clothing manufacturer is genuine?**
Check their GST registration on the official GST portal, ask for a factory address and visit or video call the floor, request references from current clients, and order a paid sample before any bulk order.

**Should I pay a clothing manufacturer 100% in advance?**
It is safer to avoid paying everything upfront to a new supplier. Common arrangements are a deposit to start production and the balance after you approve the finished goods, ideally after an inspection.

**What should I check in a garment sample?**
Check measurements against your size chart, fabric weight and feel, stitching quality, print or embroidery quality, colour accuracy, and how the piece behaves after a few washes.

**What are the biggest red flags with clothing suppliers?**
Refusing samples, unclear or changing prices, no written purchase order, no verifiable address or GST details, pressure for full advance payment, and vague answers about who actually makes your goods.

**Can someone vet suppliers for me?**
Yes. Sourcing partners like Voz Cruda match brands with manufacturers based on product capability and quantity, and coordinate production so you are not managing every supplier conversation yourself.

# India's Apparel Manufacturing Hubs: Tiruppur, Surat, Jaipur and Beyond

URL: https://vozcruda.com/india-apparel-manufacturing-hubs.html
Updated: 2026-10-24

**Short answer:** Source knitwear like t-shirts and hoodies from **Tiruppur**, synthetics, sarees and dress materials from **Surat**, block-printed ethnic wear from **Jaipur**, winterwear and hosiery from **Ludhiana**, fashion and private label from **Delhi NCR**, and woven and denim garments from **Bengaluru** and nearby clusters. Matching your product to its hub usually means better prices, faster sampling and more experienced factories.

India's apparel industry is not one market. It is a set of specialised clusters, each built over decades around particular fabrics, skills and buyers. A factory in Tiruppur that makes excellent cotton tees may be the wrong partner for a printed kurta, and a Jaipur unit known for hand block printing is not where you go for fleece hoodies.

## Garment hubs in India: what to source where

| Hub | State | Best known for |
|---|---|---|
| Tiruppur | Tamil Nadu | Cotton knitwear: t-shirts, polos, hoodies, sweatshirts, innerwear, kidswear |
| Surat | Gujarat | Synthetic fabrics, sarees, dress materials, woven and ethnic apparel |
| Jaipur | Rajasthan | Block-printed and hand-finished ethnic wear, kurtas, dresses, home textiles |
| Ludhiana | Punjab | Woollens, sweaters, knitted winterwear, hosiery |
| Delhi NCR | Delhi, UP, Haryana | Export garments, women's fashion, private label, embroidery |
| Bengaluru | Karnataka | Woven garments, shirts, trousers, denim, contemporary apparel |
| Kolkata | West Bengal | Hosiery, innerwear, budget knitwear and kidswear |
| Mumbai | Maharashtra | Fashion and wovens, women's wear, wholesale markets |

## Tiruppur: India's knitwear capital

If your brand sells t-shirts, polos, hoodies, sweatshirts or joggers, Tiruppur is usually the first stop. The cluster covers the full knit chain, from knitting and dyeing to printing, stitching and finishing, which makes it efficient for cotton basics.

- **Good for:** 180 to 300 GSM cotton tees, French terry and fleece, kidswear, private label basics.
- **Keep in mind:** many units are export-focused with higher MOQs. Pooled lots help small brands get in.

Read our [Tiruppur buyer's guide](https://vozcruda.com/tiruppur-garment-manufacturing-guide.html) for how the cluster works, or the guide to [small-batch t-shirt manufacturing](https://vozcruda.com/small-batch-t-shirt-manufacturing-india.html).

## Surat: synthetics and ethnic fabrics

Surat is a major centre for synthetic and blended fabrics, and for sarees and dress materials. It suits brands working with polyester, viscose blends, georgette and crepe.

- **Good for:** ethnic wear, sarees, dress materials, women's western wear in synthetic fabrics.
- **Keep in mind:** fabric choice is huge, so be specific about composition and finish.

## Jaipur: prints and hand-finished ethnic wear

Jaipur and nearby towns like Sanganer and Bagru are known for hand block printing, and for ethnic and fusion wear with handwork.

- **Good for:** printed kurtas, co-ord sets, dresses, cotton ethnic wear.
- **Keep in mind:** hand processes create natural variation and longer lead times. Build them into your launch plan.

## Ludhiana: winterwear and woollens

Ludhiana is India's main hub for sweaters, woollen and acrylic knitwear, and hosiery.

- **Good for:** sweaters, cardigans, knitted winterwear, thermal and hosiery products.
- **Keep in mind:** demand is seasonal. Book production well before winter.

## Delhi NCR: fashion and private label

Noida, Gurugram, Okhla and surrounding areas host many export houses and fashion manufacturers, with strong embroidery and embellishment skills.

- **Good for:** women's fashion, private label, embroidered and embellished pieces, fusion wear.
- **Keep in mind:** range is wide, so vet each unit for your specific category.

## Bengaluru: wovens, denim and a growing brand scene

Bengaluru has long been a large garment manufacturing cluster, especially for woven garments. It is also home to a growing community of D2C fashion brands, and to Voz Cruda.

- **Good for:** shirts, trousers, denim, contemporary casualwear.
- **Keep in mind:** many large units are export-focused; smaller units serve domestic brands.

## Kolkata and Mumbai

**Kolkata** has a large hosiery and innerwear industry and serves value-focused knitwear and kidswear. **Mumbai** combines fashion design, woven manufacturing and big wholesale markets, useful for women's wear and fast-moving fashion.

## How to choose the right hub

- **Start from the fabric.** Knit cotton points to Tiruppur, synthetics to Surat, wool to Ludhiana, hand prints to Jaipur.
- **Consider decoration.** Embroidery-heavy designs often suit Delhi NCR; block prints suit Jaipur.
- **Check your quantity.** Export-focused units have higher MOQs. Domestic-focused units or pooled lots suit small runs.
- **Vet the specific unit.** A hub's reputation does not guarantee every factory. Use our [supplier vetting checklist](https://vozcruda.com/how-to-vet-apparel-suppliers.html).

Not sure which hub fits your product? [Share your requirement](https://vozcruda.com/#contact) and Voz Cruda will match you with suitable units across India.

## Frequently asked questions

**Which is the biggest garment hub in India?**
It depends on the product. Tiruppur is the best-known hub for cotton knitwear, Delhi NCR and Bengaluru have large clusters of export garment factories, and Surat leads in synthetic textiles. Pick the hub that specialises in your garment rather than the one that sounds biggest.

**Which city in India is best for t-shirt manufacturing?**
Tiruppur in Tamil Nadu is India's best-known knitwear hub and the usual first choice for cotton t-shirts, polos, hoodies and other knit basics.

**Where are ethnic wear manufacturers concentrated in India?**
Jaipur is known for block-printed and hand-finished ethnic wear, while Surat is a major centre for sarees, dress materials and synthetic ethnic fabrics. Delhi NCR also has many ethnic and fusion wear units.

**Which Indian city is known for winterwear?**
Ludhiana in Punjab is India's main centre for woollens, sweaters, knitted winterwear and hosiery.

**Where is denim made in India?**
Ahmedabad is home to several large denim fabric mills, and garment units in Bengaluru, Delhi NCR and Ballari produce jeans and other denim garments.

**Do I need to visit a hub to source from it?**
Not necessarily. Many buyers source remotely through samples and video calls, or through a sourcing partner. Voz Cruda matches your product to suitable units across these hubs and coordinates production.

# Custom T-Shirts in Small Quantities: A Guide to Low MOQ T-Shirt Manufacturing in India

URL: https://vozcruda.com/small-batch-t-shirt-manufacturing-india.html
Updated: 2026-10-10

**Short answer:** To make custom t-shirts in small quantities in India: choose your fabric and GSM (for example 240 GSM cotton for an oversized fit), pick a print method that suits small runs (DTF or DTG for many colours, screen print for bold few-colour designs), approve a sample, then produce through a low MOQ route. Pooled lots on Smallotz let you order factory-made tees in small quantities at close to bulk pricing.

## Step 1: Choose the fabric

Fabric decides how your tee feels, drapes and lasts. The most common options:

| Fabric | Feel | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| 100% cotton single jersey | Soft, breathable | Everyday and oversized tees |
| Combed cotton | Smoother, more even than carded | Premium basics |
| Bio-washed cotton | Softer, less pilling | Premium feel at a small extra cost |
| Cotton-polyester blend | Less shrinkage, quicker drying | Merchandise, team and event wear |
| Polyester (dri-fit) | Light, moisture-wicking | Sportswear and activewear |

## Step 2: Pick the right GSM

Our [fabric guide](https://vozcruda.com/fabric-guide-for-clothing-brands.html) covers GSM for every product.

GSM (grams per square metre) measures fabric weight. Heavier fabric feels more premium and holds structure; lighter fabric is cooler.

- **160 to 180 GSM:** light everyday tees, summer wear, merchandise.
- **180 to 220 GSM:** mid-weight regular-fit tees with a quality feel.
- **220 to 260+ GSM:** heavyweight oversized streetwear tees with a structured drape.

## Step 3: Decide the fit

- **Regular:** classic fit, works for most customers.
- **Oversized:** dropped shoulders, wider body and longer sleeves. Popular in streetwear.
- **Boxy:** wide and slightly cropped.
- **Slim:** closer to the body, often with some stretch.

Write measurements for every size in a tech pack. Our [tech pack guide](https://vozcruda.com/tech-pack-guide-for-beginners.html) shows the key points to measure, and the [t-shirt tech pack example](https://vozcruda.com/tech-pack-example-t-shirt.html) shows a complete size chart.

## Step 4: Choose a print method

For a deeper comparison, read [screen printing vs DTF vs DTG](https://vozcruda.com/screen-printing-vs-dtf-vs-dtg-india.html).

| Method | Best for | Small batch fit | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Screen printing | Bold designs with few colours | Good from moderate quantities | Very durable; each colour needs a screen |
| DTF (direct to film) | Multi-colour and detailed designs | Excellent | No screens; works on cotton and blends |
| DTG (direct to garment) | Photographic, full-colour art | Excellent | Best on cotton; softer hand-feel |
| Puff print | Raised, textured graphics | Moderate | Popular in streetwear |
| Embroidery | Logos, small premium details | Good | Cost depends on stitch count |

## What drives t-shirt cost

- **Fabric and GSM:** heavier and combed or bio-washed cotton costs more.
- **Quantity:** setup costs spread over more pieces means a lower unit price. This is why pooling helps.
- **Colours:** custom dyed colours can carry dye-lot minimums.
- **Decoration:** number of print colours, print size and placements.
- **Branding:** custom neck labels, hang tags and packaging.

## How to order a small batch of custom tees

- Finalise fabric, GSM, fit, colours and print in a simple tech pack.
- Join or start a pooled t-shirt lot on Smallotz, or request a direct quote if you need 300+ pieces per style.
- Approve a sample: measure it, wash it and check print quality.
- Confirm quantity, size split and delivery date in writing.
- Check pieces on arrival, then reorder the colours and sizes that sell.

## Where t-shirts are made in India

Tiruppur in Tamil Nadu is India's best-known knitwear cluster and the usual choice for cotton tees, from fabric knitting to printing and stitching. Kolkata and Ludhiana also produce knitwear. See our guide to [India's apparel hubs](https://vozcruda.com/india-apparel-manufacturing-hubs.html) and our [Tiruppur buyer's guide](https://vozcruda.com/tiruppur-garment-manufacturing-guide.html).

Ready to make your first batch? [Open Smallotz](https://smallotz.vozcruda.com/) or read the full [low MOQ clothing guide](https://vozcruda.com/low-moq-clothing-manufacturers-india.html).

## Frequently asked questions

**What is the MOQ for custom t-shirts in India?**
Many factories ask for 300 to 1,000 pieces per style for fully custom t-shirts, often with a per-colour minimum. Small units accept less at a higher price, and pooled lots on Smallotz let you order smaller quantities at close to bulk pricing.

**What GSM is best for an oversized t-shirt?**
Oversized streetwear tees are commonly made in 220 to 260 GSM cotton for a heavier, structured drape. Regular-fit everyday tees are often 160 to 200 GSM.

**Which printing method is best for small batches?**
DTF and DTG are cost-effective for small runs and multi-colour designs because they need no screens. Screen printing gives excellent durability and becomes cheaper per piece as quantity grows, especially for designs with few colours.

**What is bio-washed cotton?**
Bio-washing is an enzyme treatment that removes loose surface fibres from cotton. It gives the fabric a smoother, softer feel and reduces pilling.

**How long does it take to make custom t-shirts?**
After sample approval, small batches of custom tees typically take a few weeks, depending on fabric availability, dyeing and printing. Add time for sampling and, with pooled orders, for the lot to fill.

# What Is a Tech Pack? Meaning, What to Include and How to Make One

URL: https://vozcruda.com/tech-pack-guide-for-beginners.html
Updated: 2026-10-24

**Short answer:** A **tech pack** (short for technical package) is the blueprint a factory uses to make your garment. It includes flat sketches, a size chart with measurements and tolerances, fabric and GSM, trims, colours, artwork placement, labels and packing instructions. A clear tech pack means accurate quotes, fewer sample rounds and bulk production that matches what you approved.

Most problems between new brands and factories come down to assumptions. You imagined a dropped shoulder; they made a regular one. You wanted a 2 cm rib; they used 1.5 cm. A tech pack removes the guesswork by putting every decision on paper.

## What is a tech pack?

Think of a tech pack as the recipe for one garment. A photo or a reference piece shows a factory what you like. A tech pack tells them exactly what to make: which fabric, how many centimetres for each measurement in each size, which stitch on the hem, where the print sits and how each piece is folded and packed.

The factory uses it at every stage:

- **Quoting:** fabric, GSM, trims and print method decide the cost, so a quote without a tech pack is a guess.
- **Sampling:** the pattern maker and sampling tailor work from your measurements and drawings.
- **Bulk production:** the line follows the approved version, and the quality team checks pieces against your size chart and tolerances.

Without one, every one of those steps relies on memory and WhatsApp messages, which is how a sample comes back in the wrong shade or fit.

## What goes into a tech pack

| Section | What it includes |
|---|---|
| Cover page | Style name and number, season, brand, date and version |
| Flat sketches | Front and back technical drawings, with callouts for details |
| Size chart (spec sheet) | Measurements for every size, how to measure each point, and tolerances |
| Bill of materials (BOM) | Fabric, composition, GSM, colour, plus every trim: thread, rib, buttons, zips, drawcords |
| Construction details | Stitch types, seam finishes, hem widths, neck finish |
| Artwork and placement | Print or embroidery files, sizes, colours (Pantone where possible) and exact placement |
| Labels and packaging | Neck label, wash care label, hang tag, polybag and folding instructions |
| Order sheet | Quantity per colour and size, and the delivery date you need |

Want to see every section filled in? Our [t-shirt tech pack example](https://vozcruda.com/tech-pack-example-t-shirt.html) walks through a complete one, page by page.

## The size chart: the most important page

For a t-shirt, the key measuring points are usually:

- Chest width (measured 2 to 3 cm below the armhole)
- Body length (from high point of shoulder to hem)
- Shoulder width
- Sleeve length and sleeve opening
- Armhole depth
- Neck width, neck drop and rib width
- Hem width

Give each measurement for every size, and add a tolerance, for example plus or minus 1 cm on body measurements. Tolerances turn "this looks off" into an objective check.

Write down how each point is measured too. "Chest" could mean half chest measured flat or the full circumference, and the two numbers differ by a factor of two. Most Indian factories measure garments flat, so say "half chest, measured flat" if that is what you mean.

ShortcutFind a garment you love the fit of, measure it flat, and use those numbers as your base size. Then grade up and down for other sizes, or ask the factory to grade from your base.

## Tech pack template: a page-by-page checklist

Use this as your template. If a page is blank when you send it, the factory will fill the gap with its own default. Prefer a ready-made file? [Download our free tech pack template](https://vozcruda.com/tech-pack-template.html) in Excel, Google Sheets or PDF.

- **Cover:** brand, style name, style number, version, date, contact person.
- **Flats:** front and back drawings, with arrows to every detail (rib, topstitch, pocket, label position).
- **Spec sheet:** measuring points down the side, sizes across the top, tolerance column, a small diagram showing where each point is measured.
- **BOM:** main fabric (type, composition, GSM, colour), rib or contrast fabric, thread, and every trim with size and colour.
- **Construction:** seam type for side, shoulder and sleeve, hem finish and width, neck finish, any taping or reinforcement.
- **Artwork:** print or embroidery method, artwork size in cm, colour references, placement measured from a fixed point.
- **Labels and packing:** neck or printed label, care label content and position, hang tag, fold, polybag, size sticker, carton marking.
- **Order sheet:** colour by size quantities, target delivery date, delivery address.

## How to make a tech pack without a designer

- **Collect references:** photos of garments with the fit, fabric and details you want.
- **Draw flats:** simple front and back outlines. Free templates and tools like Canva or Google Slides work for a first version.
- **Measure a reference garment** and build your size chart.
- **List materials:** fabric type, composition, GSM, colours and every trim. Our [fabric and GSM guide](https://vozcruda.com/fabric-guide-for-clothing-brands.html) explains the terms.
- **Add artwork:** high-resolution files with placement measured from fixed points, such as "8 cm below the neck seam, centred."
- **Specify labels and packing.**
- **Version it:** every change after a sample gets a new version number and date.

If you do hire a freelance designer or technical designer, prices vary a lot with the garment's complexity and the number of sizes. Ask whether the fee includes size grading and revisions after the first sample, because those are where extra charges usually appear.

## Tech pack vs spec sheet vs BOM

Factories and designers use these words loosely, so it helps to know what each one usually means.

| Term | What it usually means | Enough on its own? |
|---|---|---|
| Tech pack | The full package: drawings, measurements, materials, construction, artwork, labels, packing | Yes, for a new style |
| Spec sheet | The measurement table and tolerances, sometimes with a sketch | Only when the base product already exists |
| BOM | The list of every material and trim, with quantities | No, it is one section of the tech pack |

## Tech packs for pooled and private label orders

If you join a pooled lot or build on a manufacturer's existing product, much of the tech pack already exists: fabric, construction and base measurements are fixed for the lot. You only need a short spec sheet covering what is yours, such as quantity and size split, colour where offered, print artwork and placement, and labels. It is one more reason pooling is a quick way to launch. Read [how private label works](https://vozcruda.com/private-label-clothing-brand-india.html) for more on building on an existing product.

## Common tech pack mistakes

- **Missing tolerances,** so there is no agreed standard for quality checks.
- **Vague placement** like "print on chest" instead of measured positions.
- **No colour references,** leading to the wrong shade. Use Pantone codes or physical swatches.
- **Unspecified GSM or composition,** so the fabric feels different from what you imagined.
- **Unclear measuring method,** such as not saying whether chest is half or full.
- **Old versions in circulation.** Always send the latest version and say what changed.
- **Forgetting labels and packing,** which leads to last-minute delays.

## From tech pack to production

Send your tech pack with your quote request. Review the first sample against it point by point, record changes in a new version, and approve a final pre-production sample before bulk. See [the clothing sampling process](https://vozcruda.com/clothing-sampling-process-india.html) for how samples are reviewed round by round, and our [supplier vetting guide](https://vozcruda.com/how-to-vet-apparel-suppliers.html) for how to check them. When you are ready, [share your tech pack with Voz Cruda](https://vozcruda.com/#contact) for matching and a quote.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is a tech pack in clothing?**
A tech pack is a document that gives a manufacturer everything needed to make a garment: technical drawings, measurements for every size, fabric, trims, colours, artwork placement, labels and packing instructions.

**What does tech pack stand for?**
Tech pack is short for technical package. It is the technical package of drawings and specifications that goes from a brand to a factory.

**Do I need a tech pack for a small order?**
Yes. Even for small quantities, a tech pack reduces misunderstandings and sampling rounds. For pooled or private label orders built on an existing product, a shorter spec sheet covering your changes is often enough.

**What is the difference between a tech pack and a spec sheet?**
A spec sheet is usually one part of a tech pack: the table of measurements and tolerances for each size. The full tech pack adds drawings, materials, construction, artwork, labels and packing.

**Can I make a tech pack without a designer?**
Yes. You can start from a garment you like, measure it, sketch flat drawings with simple tools and list fabric, trims and artwork details. Many founders do their first tech pack themselves.

**What software is used to make tech packs?**
Many designers use Adobe Illustrator for flat sketches and spreadsheets or PDF layouts for specifications. Simple tech packs can be made in Google Slides, Canva or Excel. Send the factory a PDF so the layout does not shift.

**How many pages is a tech pack?**
A simple t-shirt tech pack can fit on four to six pages. Garments with more parts, such as jackets, shirts or lined dresses, need more pages for construction details and trims.

**What is a measurement tolerance in a tech pack?**
Tolerance is the allowed difference between your specified measurement and the finished garment, such as plus or minus 1 cm. Agreeing tolerances upfront makes quality checks objective.

# Print-on-Demand vs Low MOQ Manufacturing: Which Is Right for Your Clothing Brand?

URL: https://vozcruda.com/print-on-demand-vs-low-moq-manufacturing.html
Updated: 2026-10-10

**Short answer:** Use **print-on-demand** to test designs with no stock and no upfront cost. Move to **low MOQ manufacturing** when you want better margins, your own fabric and fit, and a branded unboxing. Pooled lots on Smallotz make that move possible without committing to a factory's full minimum.

## How each model works

**Print-on-demand (POD):** a printer holds stock blank garments. When a customer orders, they print your design on one piece and ship it. You hold no inventory.

**Low MOQ manufacturing:** you have a small batch of garments made to your specifications, such as fabric, fit, colour, print and labels. You hold the stock and ship it yourself or through a fulfilment partner.

## Side-by-side comparison

| Factor | Print-on-demand | Low MOQ manufacturing |
|---|---|---|
| Upfront cost | Almost none | Cost of a small batch |
| Stock risk | None | Low, if you order conservatively |
| Margin per piece | Lower | Higher |
| Fabric, GSM and fit | Limited to the printer's blanks | Your choice |
| Print methods | Usually DTG or DTF | Screen, DTF, puff, embroidery and more |
| Branding | Often limited labels and packaging | Your neck labels, tags and packaging |
| Delivery speed | Made after each order | Ships from your stock |
| Product uniqueness | Low | High |

## When print-on-demand makes sense

- You are testing whether your designs sell at all.
- You have a large catalogue of designs with low sales per design.
- You are a creator selling occasional merchandise.

## When low MOQ manufacturing makes sense

- A few styles sell consistently and you want better margins on them.
- Your brand depends on fabric, fit or feel, such as heavyweight oversized tees.
- You want branded labels, tags and packaging.
- You want faster dispatch from your own stock.

## Signs it is time to switch

- Your best designs sell week after week.
- After POD costs and ads, there is little profit left.
- Reviews mention fabric quality or fit.
- You want to sell to boutiques or wholesale buyers, who expect consistent stock.

## How to make the switch without big risk

- **Move only your bestsellers** to production first. Keep POD for testing.
- **Order small:** enough for 6 to 10 weeks of sales.
- **Use a pooled lot** to get factory quality at close to bulk pricing without the full MOQ. Read [how MOQ aggregation works](https://vozcruda.com/what-is-moq-aggregation.html).
- **Upgrade the product:** better fabric, your fit, your labels. Give customers a reason to notice.
- **Reorder fast** when stock runs low.

Ready to move your bestsellers into production? [Open Smallotz](https://smallotz.vozcruda.com/) or read the [small-batch t-shirt guide](https://vozcruda.com/small-batch-t-shirt-manufacturing-india.html).

## Frequently asked questions

**Is print-on-demand good for starting a clothing brand?**
It is a good way to test designs with no stock risk. Its limits are lower margins, generic blank garments and less control over quality and packaging, which make it harder to build a premium brand.

**When should I move from print-on-demand to manufacturing?**
Consider switching when a few designs sell consistently, when margins are too thin to fund marketing, or when customers ask for better fabric, fit or packaging than print-on-demand can offer.

**Is low MOQ manufacturing risky?**
You do hold stock, so the risk is unsold inventory. Low MOQ keeps that risk small: you buy only what you expect to sell in the next few weeks and reorder what works.

**Can I combine print-on-demand and low MOQ production?**
Yes. Many brands produce proven bestsellers in low MOQ batches for better margins, and keep print-on-demand for testing new designs.
